## 5.4 The Doctrine of Vicarious Liability and the Corporate Accountability of AI Developers

Furthermore, the application of the doctrine of strict product liability as mandated in international consumer protection discourse—now reinforced within cutting-edge regulatory frameworks such as the *EU Artificial Intelligence Act 2024* (specifically Article 5 concerning prohibited AI practices involving subliminal manipulation, and Article 50 regarding interaction transparency and synthetic content tagging) alongside the Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27/2022)—demands that the burden of proof no longer rests upon the shoulders of vulnerable victims, but is instead systematically shifted onto the corporate giants operating behind the scenes. This philosophical and juridical transition triggers a fundamental question that challenges the very foundations of modern civil law dogmatics: how do we measure fault (*schuld*) or liability when the entity causing the harm is not a human endowed with free will and conscience (*mens rea*), but rather a wave of mathematical probabilities operating within a latent space of millions of dimensions devoid of existential consciousness? It is precisely here that the doctrine of vicarious liability and the corporate accountability of AI developers must be radically re-examined, not merely as rigid legal instruments on paper, but as a reflection of distributive justice in a boundlessly interconnected digital era (Balkin, 2020; Calo, 2017).
